topic: Cold-air intake and cat-back exhaust, each alone (stock ECU calibration), on naturally aspirated and turbocharged engines: back-to-back chassis-dyno gains

cases.car: 2018 Honda Civic Type R (FK8, 2.0L turbocharged four-cylinder; transmission not given in summary) - DSPORT Magazine Test & Tune car
cases.change: AEM cold-air intake alone, factory ECU calibration (no reflash)
cases.measure: peak wheel horsepower, chassis dyno, DSPORT Test & Tune results table (stock baseline and intake run in the same test series)
cases.publisher: DSPORT Magazine (Test & Tune: 2018 Honda Civic Type R, Part 1)
cases.note: Summary quotes the results table: 'Test 1 AEM Intake | 297.01 WHP | 3.76 | 1.26%' against a baseline of '293.25 peak whp'. The same series lists 'Test 2 REMARK Exhaust | 296.66 WHP | 3.41 | 1.14%' (next case) and 'Test 3 Intake + Exhaust | 295.80 WHP', i.e. the two together made less than either alone. With the intake and exhaust swapped back to stock and only an ECU reflash, the car made 314.15 peak whp and 332.27 lb-ft (not an intake result, not used). Honda's 306 hp rating is from the same search summary. The table sits on dsportmag.com/?p=28306; the Part 1 article (https://dsportmag.com/the-tech/test-tune-2018-honda-civic-type-r-part-1/) shows the same tests, but one summary said its table does not print the 293.25 baseline, so which URL carries which row is not certain. No torque figures for the intake run in the summaries. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'partial'): baseline 293.25 whp appeared in two searches; gain +3.76 whp is +1.28% on the baseline, while the table's 1.26% equals gain divided by the after figure; a civicx.com FK8 owner measured 306 whp / 305 wtq stock and only +4 whp / +0 wtq from full bolt-ons on the stock tune, attributed to the ECU working to torque targets; Mishimoto claims +12.8 hp / +12.9 lb-ft for its FK8 intake on the stock tune (manufacturer, no baseline, not used).

cases.car: 2018 Honda Civic Type R (FK8, 2.0L turbocharged four-cylinder; transmission not given in summary) - DSPORT Magazine Test & Tune car (same car as above)
cases.change: REMARK FK8 Spec-III exhaust alone, factory ECU calibration (summary does not say where the system starts; reported as an exhaust-only bolt-on)
cases.measure: peak wheel horsepower, chassis dyno, DSPORT Test & Tune results table (same baseline as the intake case)
cases.publisher: DSPORT Magazine (Test & Tune: 2018 Honda Civic Type R, Part 1)
cases.note: Summary: 'A DSPORT table lists a 293.25 WHP baseline, with the REMARK exhaust test at 296.66 WHP, a gain of 3.41 WHP (about 1.14%). Test 2 REMARK Exhaust | 296.66 WHP | 3.41 | 1.14% | +3.41.' The Part 1 article names the exhaust as the REMARK FK8 Spec-III. Intake + exhaust together: 295.80 whp. No torque figures in the summary. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'partial'): single summary for the after figure, baseline shared with the intake case; 296.66 - 293.25 = 3.41 matches the stated gain (+1.16% on the baseline, 1.15% of the after figure, against 1.14% printed); a gain this size is inside typical pull-to-pull dyno variation (see ruleOfThumb).

cases.car: 2019 Subaru WRX (2.0L turbocharged flat-four; transmission not given in summary; about 35,000 miles, otherwise stock) - DSPORT Magazine Test & Tune car
cases.change: Aftermarket exhaust alone, factory ECU calibration (article text names it REMARK, the results table names ARK Design)
cases.measure: peak wheel horsepower, chassis dyno, DSPORT Test & Tune results table
cases.publisher: DSPORT Magazine (Test & Tune: 2019 Subaru WRX, Part 1: Exhaust and Accessport)
cases.note: Summary: the car is 'rated at 268 horsepower and 258 lb-ft of torque to the flywheel' and was 'completely stock with 35,000 miles'. 'One passage reports 244 peak wheel horsepower and 256 lb-ft of peak torque. A results table from what appears to be the same test series lists a baseline of 253.14 WHP.' 'The table shows an exhaust test at 260.93 WHP (+7.79, about 3.1%).' A Cobb AccessPort V3 flash is listed at 258.57 WHP and Perrin intake plus AccessPort at 273.59 WHP (not single-part changes, not used). The article says the Cobb reflash gave 'a 12.1whp gain, or a 38whp gain, depending on the factory ECU's mood'. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'partial'): weakest case on the page; the 253.14 table baseline disagrees with the text's 244 whp, the exhaust brand differs between text and table, and the summary only says the table 'appears' to belong to this test; if it does, +7.79 whp (+3.08%); the ECU's run-to-run 'mood' (12 to 38 whp spread on a reflash) is larger than the exhaust gain. Second read: the table's AccessPort row (258.57 whp) is +5.43 over 253.14 or +14.57 over 244, matching neither of the article's stated 12.1 or 38 whp reflash gains, further sign that table and text may not describe the same runs.

cases.car: 2010 Chevrolet Camaro SS (6.2L L99 V8, naturally aspirated, 6L80E 6-speed automatic) - stock owner's car lent for the test
cases.change: K&N Aircharger cold-air intake alone, factory calibration
cases.measure: rear-wheel horsepower and torque, Dynojet chassis dyno, stock and intake on the same car in one test session
cases.publisher: Chevy Hardcore / LSX Magazine ('Dyno Test: 4 K&N vs. AEM 5th Gen Camaro Intake Options', January 2012)
cases.note: Summary: 'A stock 2010 Camaro SS with the 400 hp L99 and 6L80E automatic was run on a Dynojet', lent by an owner in Killeen, Texas. 'The stock car made about 312.9 rwhp and 331.5 lb-ft'; 'K&N Panel Filter: About 321.4 rwhp, a gain of roughly 8.4 rwhp'; 'K&N Aircharger: About 337.9 rwhp and 352.3 lb-ft, a gain of about 25 rwhp and 20.8 lb-ft'. AEM figures were not in the summary. The summary also says 'the test was run on K&N's own equipment in a third-party article', so K&N may have hosted the test: treat with some caution. A separate Chevy Hardcore header test recorded a different stock 2010 Camaro SS at 313.1 hp at 5,800 rpm on a Mustang dyno (https://www.chevyhardcore.com/?p=358594), a useful cross-check on the baseline. Same article also at https://www.chevyhardcore.com/?p=10497. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'partial'): single summary, internally consistent (337.9 - 312.9 = 25.0 whp, +8.0%; 352.3 - 331.5 = 20.8 lb-ft, +6.3%); stock baseline matches an independent Chevy Hardcore stock 2010 SS (313.1) within 0.2 hp; K&N's own write-up for this engine claims an estimated 18 hp.

cases.car: Scion FR-S / Subaru BRZ (2.0L naturally aspirated flat-four; year, exact model and transmission not given in summary) - MotoIQ test car
cases.change: ARK Design Road Spec exhaust alone (one of several ARK systems in a shootout), factory ECU calibration
cases.measure: peak wheel horsepower and torque, chassis dyno, stock baseline and exhaust on the same car in the same shootout
cases.publisher: MotoIQ ('The Great ARK Design FR-S / BRZ Exhaust Shootout')
cases.note: Summary: 'The stock baseline was 148 hp @ 6900 rpm and 118.3 lb ft of torque at 6100 rpm. The ARK Road Spec reached 152.8 hp @ 7000 rpm, which is a gain of nearly 5 whp and 3 lb/ft of torque over stock.' The after torque is given only as 'about 3 lb-ft' more, so no after torque figure is recorded. The 200 hp / 151 lb-ft stock rating is from a Grassroots Motorsports summary (case below). MotoIQ's FR-S articles say their Superflow dyno 'typically reads about 10 hp lower than a Dynojet' (not confirmed to be the dyno used here). Other figures from the same search: Perrin's own cat-back about +7 whp (manufacturer); speed.academy's Corsa cat-back test on a 155 whp stock FR-S expected about 2 whp and noted gains this small are hard to detect; aFe and Injen claim +5 hp / +6 lb-ft and up to +7 hp / +8 lb-ft (manufacturer). Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'partial'): single summary; 152.8 - 148 = 4.8 whp ('nearly 5'), +3.2%; the shootout is of one maker's systems but the magazine ran the dyno; agrees in size with the other NA cat-back figures found (vendor +4 to +7 hp, independent 'about 2 whp'); DSPORT found on this platform that an exhaust added after an intake made no further power on the stock ECU.

cases.car: 2015 Scion FR-S (2.0L flat-four with an aftermarket turbocharger kit; boost and transmission not given in summary) - Grassroots Motorsports 'Project Copart' car
cases.change: JBA stainless cat-back exhaust (part No. 30-9030) alone, on the already-turbocharged car; one pipe shortened to clear the turbo install
cases.measure: horsepower and torque, chassis dyno (the car 'dynoed'), average of several pulls before; wheel-vs-crank label not given in summary
cases.publisher: Grassroots Motorsports ('The cork in our turbocharged FR-S build? The exhaust.')
cases.note: Quoted: 'After a few pulls, they averaged around 246 horsepower and 223 lb.-ft. of torque. That's already 46 more horsepower and 72 more torque than stock thanks to the turbocharger.' After the JBA cat-back 'the car dynoed at 263 horsepower and 240 lb-ft, a gain of 17 horsepower and 17 lb-ft', and 'the JBA system weighed 8 pounds less than the factory exhaust'. A later article on the same car lists 292 hp / 242 lb-ft with several more mods, 'an increase of 92 horses and 91 torques over the stock car's 200 horsepower and 151 lb.-ft. of torque' (not used). GRM compares its dyno figures with the factory crank rating, so the wheel label is inferred from the chassis-dyno setting rather than stated. Turbo kit make and boost psi not in the summaries. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'confirmed'): two searches agreed on 246/223 before and 263/240 after; 263 - 246 = 17 and 240 - 223 = 17 match the stated gains; +6.9% power, +7.6% torque. Second read corrected the first pass's comparison: that is about twice (not four times) the +3.2% of the naturally aspirated FR-S/BRZ ARK cat-back, and about six times the Type R's +1.2% on a factory turbo calibration.

cases.car: 2017 Honda Civic Si (10th generation, 1.5L turbocharged four-cylinder; transmission not given in summary) - PRL Motorsports 'Project Snow White'
cases.change: PRL Motorsports Stage 1 intake alone, '100% stock' car otherwise, factory ECU calibration
cases.measure: peak horsepower and torque, chassis dyno (dyno pulls of the car; the post says 'hp', not 'whp'), stock and intake on the same car
cases.publisher: PRL Motorsports (intake maker's own project-car blog)
cases.note: Intake maker's own result for its own product: a manufacturer claim. Quoted: '100% Stock Civic Si Baseline: 186 hp & 215 ft/lbs tq; 100% Stock Civic Si + Stage 1 Intake: 191 hp & 216 ft/lbs tq.' The post 'says hp, not whp', and says four dyno pulls were recorded. Recorded as wheel figures because they are chassis-dyno pulls of the car. Context from other summaries: DSPORT measured a different stock 2019 Si at 189.8 whp / 190.6 lb-ft with factory boost of roughly 18.9 psi (https://dsportmag.com/the-tech/test-n-tune/honda-civic-si-test-tune/); Mishimoto claims +4.2 whp for its Si intake on the stock tune (manufacturer); PRL elsewhere reports +4 to +9 whp from a drop-in filter and intake hose without a tune. Read from search-result summary; page not opened. First-pass check (was 'confirmed'): two searches agreed on 186 -> 191 hp and the second gave torque 215 -> 216; +5 hp (+2.7%), +1 lb-ft (+0.5%), power up at the top end with peak torque essentially unchanged, consistent with a torque-limited stock turbo calibration.

ruleOfThumb.claim: K&N says its intakes typically add an average of 15-25 hp over a stock system (manufacturer claim); its own Silverado test claims up to +27.1 hp and +39.0 lb-ft at 5,000 rpm, with a low-end loss noted for a closed-box design.
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'The company says its intakes typically add an average of 15-25 additional horsepower over a stock system. That is a marketing figure, not an independent result.' and 'max gain of 27.1 horsepower and 39.0-foot pounds of torque at 5,000 RPM'. Which K&N page carries the 15-25 hp line was not certain from the summary. Against the cases on this page, only the Camaro SS (+25 whp, possibly on K&N equipment) reaches that range; the independent turbo results are +4 to +5 whp. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: In an independent same-car test of four cold-air intakes, three produced no change in horsepower or torque and the fourth gained about 2 percent.
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'The author tested four cold air intakes on the same car. Three of the four produced no change in horsepower or torque, and the fourth gained about 2 percent.' The car was not named in the summary. Matches the DSPORT Type R (+1.3%) and PRL Si (+2.7%) results. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: On naturally aspirated cars a cat-back exhaust gains little: an Engineering Explained test on a Honda S2000 showed about 3 hp, mostly at higher rpm.
ruleOfThumb.note: Summary: 'One Engineering Explained test on a Honda S2000 showed about 3 hp, mostly at higher RPM. The same article concludes that for naturally-aspirated cars, the improvements are fairly minimal.' Compare the MotoIQ FR-S/BRZ ARK case (+4.8 whp, +3.2%). The same search's lower-authority blogs put intake gains at about 0-5 whp NA and 3-10 whp turbo (tpautorepair.net, threepiece.us), not used as evidence. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: Modern stock ECUs cap what bolt-ons can add: on the FR-S/BRZ the factory ECU 'has tables built in that essentially limit the amount of additional power', and on the FK8 Type R full bolt-ons on the stock tune gained only about 4 whp because the ECU works to torque targets; the gains appear after a reflash.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: DSPORT Magazine (Scion FR-S/BRZ intake test); CivicX forum (FK8 owner dyno)
ruleOfThumb.note: DSPORT summary: stock FR-S runs 'between 173 and 176 horsepower when tested on different days', the stock ECU 'capped output around 182 wheel horsepower', and an exhaust added after an intake 'didn't gain any additional power'. CivicX (https://www.civicx.com/forum/goto/post?id=504819 or nearby post; exact post not certain): stock 306 whp / 305 wtq, full bolt-ons on stock tune '+4 whp / no wtq gain', attributed to the FK8 ECU 'being based on torque targets'. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.

ruleOfThumb.claim: A single-digit dyno gain needs same-day, back-to-back pulls to mean anything: pull-to-pull variation of about 3-4 rwhp is normal, and comparisons made on different days or weeks apart can be skewed.
ruleOfThumb.publisher: Mustang6G forum (discussion of MotoIQ's Borla S-Type test); K&N Engineering (methodology note)
ruleOfThumb.note: Mustang6G summary: one user argued 'a dyno can vary from pull to pull' by the size of the 12.91 whp Borla gain, so 'back-to-back tests on the same dyno within about an hour are needed'; another replied that 'if it were statistical noise it would be 3-4 rwhp, not 12'. K&N: competitor tests are 'often performed on different days - sometimes even weeks apart'. MotoIQ also notes its Superflow dyno reads about 10 hp below a Dynojet, so absolute figures differ by dyno while same-dyno differences are what this page records. Which Mustang6G post carries which quote was not certain. Read from search-result summary; page not opened.
